props.title: Light the Wick

sections.content: **Light the Wick** (2010) stands as a pivotal entry in ski film history, marking a significant evolution in how action sports documentaries captured the raw intensity of big mountain skiing. Following the groundwork laid by **The Blizzard of AAHHH's** (1988) and Steep (2007), director Steve Jones and Teton Gravity Research pushed technical boundaries with RED digital cameras and helicopter-mounted systems. The film's revolutionary aerial tracking shots of athletes like Sage Cattabriga-Alosa and Seth Morrison charging Alaskan spines influenced countless action sports films that followed.

sections.content: The film's impact extends beyond just technical innovation. While earlier ski films like **The Art of Flight** (2011) focused primarily on trick progression, Light the Wick balanced pure action with environmental consciousness. The Alaska segment, featuring Chris Benchetler's fluid line choices through the Chugach Mountains, demonstrated a new approach to filming big mountain riding that emphasized the relationship between athlete and environment.

The film's sound design also marked a departure from traditional ski film formulas. Instead of relying solely on punk and metal soundtracks like **Hot Dog... The Movie** (1984), Light the Wick incorporated ambient sound and natural mountain acoustics to create a more immersive experience. This audio approach influenced later films like Into the Mind (2013) and **Days of My Youth** (2014). SUBHEAD: Evolution of Action Sports Cinematography

sections.content: Light the Wick's technical achievements sparked an arms race in action sports cinematography. The film's use of ultra-slow-motion photography at 1000 frames per second created previously impossible perspectives of skiing's most dynamic moments. This influenced later works like **The Dream Factory** (2012) and **McConkey** (2013), which pushed camera technology even further with innovative drone work and point-of-view perspectives.
